questionStem: A 52-year-old man with a 5-year history of essential hypertension comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has read about a clinical trial for a new medication, drug X, which has shown promise in controlling difficult cases of hypertension, and inquires about participation . His hypertension is moderately controlled with a thiazide diuretic, 13-adrenergic blocking agent, and calcium-channel blocking agent. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate study design?

choices.C: Randomized controlled trial of drug X versus a placebo
choices.D: Randomized controlled trial of drug X versus standard therapy

correctExplanation: To evaluate the effectiveness of a new therapy, it should be compared against the current standard. This is classically done using a randomized, double-blinded controlled trial, in which patients are enrolled into two groups: experimental and control. Those in the experimental arm receive the experimental therapy, and outcome measures are assessed. Those in the control arm receive the standard of care, and the same outcome measures are assessed. Neither the participants nor the researchers should be aware of which therapy they are receiving or administering/assessing to prevent the introduction of bias. Finally, analysis is performed to measure the efficacy of the new intervention as compared to the standard of care by looking at the differences in outcomes. A randomized controlled trial, when performed with minimized methodological flaw, is considered one of the highest levels of clinical evidence.
incorrectExplanation: nd C. Prospective and retrospective observational cohort studies (Choices A and B) evaluate outcomes with respect to exposures within groups of individuals sharing common characteristics. For example, a cohort study could evaluate whether exposure to asbestos increased the risk of mesothelioma by comparing two similar groups of persons: one group of shipyard and aerospace workers in which asbestos was used for flame retardant against another group of shipyard and aerospace workers in which asbestos was not used. Data can be collected as time progresses (prospective) or it can be retroactively collected on exposures and outcomes that have already occurred (retrospective). Cohort studies are primarily used in epidemiology, and relative risk is used to assess the difference between the groups . A randomized controlled trial of drug X versus a placebo (Choice C) would be a suboptimal study. This study would answer the question of whether drug X was an effective anti hypertensive but not whether drug X was equivalent to or better than the current standard of care in hypertension management. Additionally, an ethical argument can be made against comparing the new drug to a placebo when an effective drug exists, as placebo comparison would unnecessarily increase the risk of poorly controlled hypertension in the patients assigned to the placebo arm. ,.

questionStem: A 27-year-old man with moderate mental retardation is brought to the physician by his caretaker because of increasingly frequent episodes of intermittent vomiting over the past 3 weeks . The vomiting typically occurs within an hour after eating and usually contains partially digested food; no blood is noted in the vomitus . The patient's appetite seems unaffected , but he stops eating before he completes the meal. He has had a 3.6-kg (8-lb) weight loss since his last visit 6 months ago . He takes phenytoin for a seizure disorder but is otherwise healthy . His vital signs are within normal limits . His speech is not intelligible . Examination shows a 3 x 4-cm area of alopecia in the right occipitoparietal area of the scalp . Bowel sounds are present. The abdominal musculature voluntarily contracts with palpation ; no organomegaly or masses are palpated . There are minimal contractures in both upper and lower extremities and increased muscle tone . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: A history of mental retardation/intellectual disability, early satiety, post-prandial emesis, weight loss, and focal alopecia raises the possibility of hair ingestion, which can result in development of a gastric hair bezoar. Bezoars are space-occupying masses of indigestible matter, often hair or chewing gum. Occasionally, large-volume pill ingestion can lead to a pill bezoar. Because of the space-occupying nature of the lesion in the stomach, much smaller amounts of food can be consumed prior to feelings of satiety. If large enough, a bezoar can lead to a gastric outlet obstruction which results in vomiting of undigested food with resultant weight loss from malnutrition. The presence of alopecia raises suspicion for hair ingestion and provides a clue to the contents of the bezoar. Treatment includes supportive care to correct fluid, electrolyte, and nutritional deficiencies, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy or surgery to diagnose and remove the bezoar.
incorrectExplanation: nd L. Achalasia (Choice A) is a type of esophageal dysmotility disorder resulting from deficient peristalsis along the length of the esophagus and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. It manifests as dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, halitosis, and regurgitation of undigested food. It is diagnosed through a barium swallow plus esophageal manometry. Brain tumors (Choice B), especially if causing increased intracranial pressure, can result in vomiting and weight loss; however, this patient manifests no additional signs of increased intracranial pressure such as somnolence or altered mental status, headaches when supine, papilledema, and/or new or changing neurologic deficits. He has positive symptoms to suggest an alternate cause such as a bezoar, making brain tumor a less likely diagnosis. Bulimia nervosa (Choice C) is marked by binge-purge behaviors such as eating a large meal, then inducing vomiting. Cholecystitis (Choice D) presents acutely with fever, nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, and a Murphy sign on exam, often in the presence of gallstones. Diabetic gastroparesis (Choice E) occurs secondary to neurologic dysfunction of the enteric nervous system and typically presents late in the course of chronically uncontrolled diabetes as epigastric and left upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Drug toxicity (Choice F) has many manifestations. Several medications have known gastrointestinal adverse effects, for example, metformin, chemotherapeutics, and antibiotics. Phenytoin does have gastrointestinal adverse effects which can include nausea, vomiting, and occasionally hepatitis; however, toxicity of the drug can also include nystagmus, ataxia, vertigo, peripheral neuropathy, megaloblastic anemia, gingival hyperplasia, dysrhythmia, and hirsutism. Food poisoning (Choice G) commonly refers to the ingestion of a preformed toxin, such as Staphylococcus aureus exotoxin, or to the ingestion of food contaminated with a gastrointestinal pathogen such as Salmonella species or rotavirus. Symptoms are typically acute and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea, and are often self-limited. Gastric carcinoma (Choice I) presents with early satiety, weight loss, nausea, and vomiting if the lesion creates an obstruction to peristalsis. Physical exam may show a palpable mass, or a Sister Mary Joseph nodule. Symptoms are chronic and often occur in older persons, smokers, or those who have frequently ingested nitrate-containing foods.

questionStem: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and right knee pain. She has not had cough , abdominal pain, or pain with urination . There is no history of intravenous drug use. She appears uncomfortable . Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a few raised erythematous papules on both palms. The right knee is warm, erythematous , and tender to palpation . There is a moderate-sized effusion . Passive flexion of the knee is limited to 30 degrees because of severe pain. Analysis of synovial fluid aspirated from the right knee shows a leukocyte count of 45,000/mm 3 (80% segmented neutrophils and 20% lymphocytes) . A Gram stain of the synovial fluid and microscopic examination for crystals are negative . Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?

choices.A: A contiguous soft tissue infection of the joint by Staphylococcus aureus
choices.B: Immunologic-mediated arthritis secondary to Borrelia burgdorferi
choices.C: Immunologic-mediated arthritis secondary to group A streptococcus
choices.D: Infection of the joint secondary to disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi
choices.E: Infection of the joint secondary to disseminated Neisseria gono"hoeae

correctExplanation: Disseminated gonococcal infection presents with fever, myalgias, tenosynovitis, pustular rash often involving the palms or soles, and septic arthritis, which is occasionally polyarticular and migratory. Diagnosis is made via clinical history and examination plus aspiration of potentially septic joints . Synovial fluid analysis classically shows leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance, and the leukocyte count is often greater than 50,000/mm 3• Organisms are often visualized on gram stain. Treatment is with antibiotics and further diagnostic investigation to determine the extent of the sexually transmitted infection, including a pelvic exam in sexually active women .
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Contiguous soft tissue infection spreading to a joint by Staphylococcus aureus (Choice A) is a well-evidenced mechanism of septic arthritis; however, it would not explain the disseminated findings of rash on the palms or soles. Additionally, the history would likely include trauma to the joint in question, or several days of preceding localized skin or soft tissue infection. Immunologic-mediated arthritis secondary to Borrelia burgdorferi or group A streptococcus (Choices Band C) more often demonstrates lymphocytic predominance and an absence of organisms on synovial fluid analysis. Lymphocyte count is typically less than 50,000/mm 3• Infection of a joint secondary to disseminated Borrelia burgdorferi (Choice D) would be expected to be accompanied by a rash in the pattern of erythema migrans, history of tick exposure, and with signs of disseminated Lyme disease such as myocarditis, neuropathy , and meningitis. ,.

He was hospitalized for treatment of a similar episode 1 year ago; ultrasonography and CT scan of the abdomen at that time showed no abnormalities . His temperature is 39.3°C (102.?°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/84 mm Hg. Examination shows jaundice and epigastric tenderness without masses or rebound. questionStem: A 65-year-old man comes to the physician because of easy fatigability for 2 months. In 1985, he had loss of appetite, mild nausea , and fatigue approximately 2 months after receiving a transfusion for a bleeding peptic ulcer. The liver has a span of 12 cm. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Laboratory studies show:

choices.A: Acute cholecystitis F) Chronic hepatitis C
choices.C: Autoimmune chronic active hepatitis H) Hepatolenticular degeneration (Wilson disease)
choices.D: Budd-Chiari syndrome I) Primary biliary cirrhosis
choices.E: Chronic hepatitis B J) Sclerosing cholangitis
choices.F: The liver has a span of 12 cm. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Laboratory studies show:

The acute variant typically presents with symptoms of fatigue, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and right upper quadrant discomfort. Some patients will recover and show no evidence of ongoing infection, whereas others will never completely eliminate the virus. They may mount chronic symptoms, and untreated infection can eventually lead to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease. Hepatitis B and Care commonly transmitted via blood or sexual intercourse, with transfusion in the prescreening era being a common source of inoculation. Chronic symptoms are often nonspecific, and include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss. Physical examination may show jaundice, an enlarged or tender liver, ascites, and/or encephalopathy depending on the severity. Laboratory evaluation may show elevations in ALT or AST, hyperbilirubinemia, or coagulopathy. Anti-HCV antibodies are usually present, which does not confer immunity, along with a detectable Hepatitis C viral load.

Acute cholecystitis (Choice A) presents with fever, abdominal pain, and tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant, often in a patient with a history of gallstones. It is occasionally preceded by symptoms of biliary colic. Jaundice is a less common finding and suggests an alternate, or complicated, diagnosis such as choledocholithiasis or ascending cholangitis. Acute pancreatitis (Choice B) presents with epigastric abdominal pain, nausea, and emesis, often in a patient with a history of gallstones, alcohol use disorder, trauma, hypertriglyceridemia, or hypercalcemia. It can be complicated by necrosis, hemorrhage, abscess, or the formation of pseudocysts. It is not commonly associated with inflammatory bowel disease. Laboratory evaluation often reveals increased lipase. Autoimmune hepatitis (Choice C) presents in a range from asymptomatic to fulminant hepatitis; typically, the presentation includes chronic nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss, jaundice, nausea, vomiting, pruritis, and right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort. An enlarged, tender liver is sometimes found on examination. It is most often seen in females, often in middle age. Laboratory evaluation reveals transaminase elevation, and often an increased anti-smooth muscle antibody.

questionStem: A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever and rash for 2 days . He just completed a 6-week course of nafcillin for treatment of staphylococcal bacterial endocarditis. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F) . Examination shows a faint maculopapular rash. Cardiac examination shows an unchanged murmur of aortic insufficiency and no embolic lesions . Laboratory studies and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely set of findings on urinalysis?
correctExplanation: Interstitial nephritis is a cause of intrinsic renal failure, and often occurs secondary to medication use, with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics, and sulfas being common precipitants. It is characterized by decreased glomerular filtration rate, rising creatinine, and eosinophilic infiltrates seen on biopsy and detected on urinalysis. Patients will have a history of medication exposure and classically present with low grade fever and diffuse rash. Urinalysis typically reveals eosinophiluria, with occasional WBC casts, increased WBC/hpf, and proteinuria. Treatment involves discontinuing the inciting agent.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute tubular necrosis often follows an ischemic or nephrotoxic insult and is commonly seen in patients with cardiac arrest following prolonged resuscitation prior to return of spontaneous circulation and in patients with prolonged cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive, or hypovolemic shock. Nephrotoxic agents such as heavy metals and myoglobin can also precipitate acute tubular necrosis. It is characterized on urinalysis by proteinuria, increased WBC/hpf, muddy brown casts, and visualized tubular epithelial cells on urine microscopy {Choice A). Choice C generally reflects a normal urinalysis, with specific gravity, glucose, protein, white and red cells, and casts all within normal limits. Choice D may reflect pyelonephritis, as WBC casts and bacteria are present. Classically, the number of white cells per high power field along with leukocyte esterase and nitrites are also increased in pyelonephritis. Nephritic syndrome typically presents with red blood cell casts and hematuria {Choice E). Choice F may reflect poorly controlled diabetes or a patient taking a sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitor (e.g., canagliflozin) based on the presence of glucosuria, along with a concomitant urinary tract infection given the presence of increased WBCs and bacteria.

questionStem: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive fatigue and shortness of breath on exertion . He has not had difficulty breathing at night or chest pain. In addition to a heart murmur that was diagnosed when he was in high school , he has diverticulosis and mild osteoarthritis . He takes no medications except a daily multivitamin . He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 68 kg (150 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m 2• His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 82/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 135/90 mm Hg.There is no jugular venous distention . The carotid pulse has a slow upstroke . The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard best at the right sternal border and radiates to the apex. There is no change in the murmur with the Valsalva maneuver . There is a paradoxical splitting of S 2 and a prominent apical impulse . An ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy ; there is no evidence of infarction . Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's heart murmur?
correctExplanation: Congenital bicuspid aortic valve classically presents with early signs and symptoms of aortic stenosis and left-sided diastolic heart failure. Patients may complain of fatigue, shortness of breath, cough, diminished exercise tolerance, or syncope with exertion. Exam findings include a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at the upper right sternal border, and pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed) may be noted on examination of peripheral pulses. Because of the chronic increased afterload from a fixed obstruction by the valve, left ventricular hypertrophy and resultant diastolic dysfunction can occur. If early aortic stenosis occurs, the patient may be a candidate for aortic valve replacement.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Atrial septal defect (Choice A) presents with fixed splitting of the S2 heart sound and is caused by a failure of closure of the embryologic connection between the right and left atria. Blood generally flows from the left atrium into the right atrium, increasing the amount within the right heart and pulmonary circuit. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (Choice C) classically presents with a systolic murmur loudest in the lower left sternal border, which is quieter with increased preload and afterload. It is caused by hypertrophy of the septum, creating an outflow obstruction within the left ventricular outflow tract. It classically presents with syncope or sudden cardiac death in an exercising young athlete with a family history of a similar event. Myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve (Choice D) can eventually lead to mitral insufficiency, which presents with a holosystolic murmur; however, this condition would not be expected to cause left ventricular hypertrophy or pulsus parvus et tardus. Rheumatic heart disease (Choice E) commonly causes insufficiency murmurs in the acute phase and stenotic murmurs later in life, predominantly affecting the mitral valve. Rheumatic fever typically presents with joint inflammation, pancarditis, subcutaneous inflammatory nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea. Mitral stenosis itself presents with a diastolic murmur radiating to the axilla. If severe enough, it can result in left atrial enlargement, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation and flutter.

questionStem: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of temperatures to 39.4 °C (103°F) and shortness of breath and a 6-hour history of chest pain exacerbated by cough or inspiration . Three days ago , she started treatment with erythromycin for fever and cough productive of yellow sputum , but she discontinued the medication 24 hours later because of nausea and vomiting . She has autoimmune hepatitis that has been in remission for 3 years . She appears lethargic . Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 32/min , and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. There is dullness to percussion over the left hemithorax two thirds of the way up from the lung bases. Breath sounds are decreased at the left base. Cardiac examination shows a hyperdynamic precordium with no rubs, gallops , or murmurs . Thoracentesis is performed . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Admission to the coronary care unit
choices.C: Instillation of talc in the pleural space

correctExplanation: Hematocrit Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Bands Lymphocytes Pleural fluid Leukocyte count pH Glucose Total protein Lactate dehydrogenase 40% 20,000/mm 3 80% 15% 5% 50,000/mm 3 7.11 20 mg/dL 4 g/dL 400 U/L Pleural effusions are caused by multiple underlying conditions including infection such as pneumonia, malignancy such as lung cancer or mesothelioma, and increased hydrostatic pressure such as left-sided heart failure. They are clinically suspected on exam in the setting of dullness to percussion and diminished breath sounds and can be visualized on imaging including chest x-ray, CT scan, or ultrasound. Analyzing the pleural fluid can reveal an underlying cause to guide therapy. Fluid is inspected for cell counts, organisms, pH, glucose, total protein, and enzyme levels. Low pH and low glucose are indicative of increased cellular metabolism in the fluid and may indicate underlying malignancy and/or infection. Effusions can be further categorized as transudates (eg, serous fluid resulting from imbalanced hydrostatic or oncotic pressure) or exudates (eg, complex fluid resulting from pneumonia, empyema, malignancy, or inflammatory disease) using Light's criteria, which compares the pleural fluid protein and lactate dehydrogenase levels to those found in serum. Pneumonia can be complicated by simple parapneumonic exudative effusions, which, if sufficiently large, can compress lung parenchyma and impair respiratory mechanics. If not treated, secondary infection can occur within the pleural space leading to an empyema which requires evacuation via a chest tube or surgery in addition to continued antibiotic therapy. Empyema is characterized by an exudative effusion with increased pleural fluid leukocytes, low pH, low glucose, increased protein, and increased lactate dehydrogenase.

questionStem: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of severe substernal chest pain for 2 hours and severe shortness of breath for 30 minutes. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with an oral hypoglycemic agent and hypertension treated with a diuretic . His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F) , pulse is 104/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 100/78 mm Hg. Jugular venous pressure is increased . Bilateral crackles are heard throughout all lung fields. An S3 and S4 gallop are heard. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. An x-ray of the chest shows bilateral perihilar infiltrates and a slightly enlarged cardiac silhouette. An ECG shows ST-segment elevation and T-wave inversion in leads V 2 through Vs- Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Myocardial infarction classically presents with acute-onset chest pain, often radiating to the neck, jaw, or arm, along with shortness of breath, nausea, and/or light-headedness. Risk factors include a history of smoking, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and/or obesity. If the infarction results in left ventricular dysfunction, patients may experience cardiogenic pulmonary edema resulting in shortness of breath, tachypnea, hypoxia, audible crackles, and an S3 or S4 gallop. Diagnosis is made using clinical history, analysis of cardiac biomarkers, and an ECG which may show ST-segment elevation or depression, inverted T-waves, or Q­ waves. Treatment requires the use of antiplatelet agents (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel) plus anticoagulants (eg, heparin), pain control, and revascularization through angioplasty, thrombolysis, or coronary artery bypass grafting. Complications include dysrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, pulmonary edema, wall rupture, and post-infarction pericarditis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute pericarditis (Choice A) occurs because of an infectious, inflammatory, or malignant precipitant, and presents as pleuritic chest pain that is exacerbated with lying down. ECG findings include diffuse (not focal) ST elevations and PR depressions. Pericardia! tamponade (Choice C) presents with hypotension, shortness of breath, distant heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and pulsus paradoxus. It occurs following accumulation of either a large volume or rapid-onset pericardia! effusion. Rapid decompression of the pericardia! space is required to prevent ongoing shock. The ECG is typically low voltage and can demonstrate electrical alternans. Pneumonia (Choice D) presents with cough, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, fever, and abnormal breath sounds. It often follows an upper respiratory infection or aspiration event and is more common in immunocompromised persons. The ECG is often unremarkable, and the chest x-ray can be normal early in the course but may show patchy multifocal infiltrates or a single area of consolidation. Pulmonary embolism (Choice E) presents with acute chest pain, shortness of breath, and hypoxia, often in a patient with deep venous thrombosis or a known hypercoagulable state. Small pulmonary emboli are often undetectable on chest x-ray, and the ECG may be normal or show sinus tachycardia. Large emboli with infarction are often seen on chest x-ray by secondary signs such as wedge-shaped areas of infarction or via the Westermark sign of unilateral oligemia. The ECG in a pulmonary embolus often shows sinus tachycardia, and if there is right heart strain can also exhibit right axis deviation, S wave in lead 1, Q wave in lead 3, and inverted Twave in lead 3 ('S1Q3T3'). ST segment elevation would not be expected.

questionStem: An 87-year-old man is admitted to the hospital for treatment of a right femoral neck fracture sustained when he fell down a staircase . He has osteoarthritis of the knees treated with ibuprofen (400 mg three times daily). He takes no other medications. He also reports memory loss, particularly in remembering the names of people he has met recently. He first noted the problem 4 years ago, and he states that it is slowly becoming worse . There is no family history of dementia . He lives alone , drives a car, does his own shopping and cooking , and manages his own finances . He does not smoke cigarettes . He drinks one beer daily. His blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Examination shows shortening and external rotation of the right lower extremity. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings . His Mini-Mental State Examination score is 27/30 . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's memory loss?
correctExplanation: Mild forgetfulness without significant impairment in ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living, with a Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score of 27/30, is most consistent with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). MCI is often seen prior to a diagnosis of dementia, especially Alzheimer type, and includes amnestic (memory-related) and non-amnestic (language, spatial, executive functional impairment) MCI with generally preserved ability to function independently without significant impairment.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice A) is defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders - fifth edition (DSM-5) as loss of intellectual function within multiple domains: language, memory, perception, motor skills, attention, orientation, problem solving, and executive function. Presumptive diagnosis involves demonstrating cognitive impairment, often through the MMSE, excluding similar syndromes (e.g., vascular dementia, Lewy Body dementia) and secondary causes such as toxic (e.g., heavy metal poisoning), metabolic (e.g., electrolyte disturbances, uremia, hyperammonemia, vitamin deficiencies), endocrine (e.g., thyroid, adrenal, and parathyroid derangement), infectious (e.g., neurosyphilis, HIV encephalopathy, meningoencephalitis), polypharmaceutical (e.g., sedative-hypnotic and anticholinergic use), and superimposed psychiatric causes (e.g., major depressive disorder). Medication adverse effect (Choice B) is a well-recognized cause of cognitive impairment that is often reversible in elderly persons. Anticholinergics and sedative-hypnotics are frequently cited as causing depressed mental status or delirium when administered to persons with limited cognitive reserve. This patient does not clearly have an abrupt cognitive decline correlated with initiating such medications. Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia (Choice D) is characterized as a stepwise decline in cognitive functioning following vascular phenomena, for example, presenting as progressive loss of function after each cerebrovascular accident in a series of ischemic strokes. Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency (Choice E) presents with dementia resulting from nutritional deficiency and is often accompanied by megaloblastic anemia.

questionStem: A 64-year-old woman with a 4-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with insulin comes to the emergency department because of exertional chest pressure for 3 weeks. The first episode occurred while she was walking upstairs and was relieved by 5 minutes of rest. The second episode occurred 1 week ago while she was mowing the lawn and was relieved after 10 minutes of rest. She had two episodes yesterday , each lasting 15 minutes; both occurred with exertion and were accompanied by shortness of breath and nausea . Today she had a 10-minute episode starting while she was in the shower and another while she was walking into the emergency department. Examination and an ECG show no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Self-monitoring of blood glucose concentration during the next episode of chest pain
choices.D: Antianginal drug therapy now and an exercise stress test in 5 days
choices.E: Admit the patient to the hospital

correctExplanation: Exertional chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath that improves with rest is suggestive of stable angina pectoris, caused by cardiac ischemia from insufficient perfusion during exertion through narrowed coronary arteries. This patient presents with worsening symptoms of angina, occurring more frequently and for a longer duration of time. This is consistent with unstable angina, defined by anginal symptoms that are new, occur at rest, or are worsening in severity. Unstable angina is a type of acute coronary syndrome, which requires admission to the hospital and urgent diagnostic workup, including serial ECGs, troponin testing, cardiology consultation, and stress test or cardiac catheterization. Patients with unstable angina are stratified based upon the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) score, which assists in identifying the need for therapeutic anticoagulation and coronary angiography.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Self-monitoring of blood glucose concentration during the next episode of chest pain (Choice A) would not be sufficient for workup of this patient's unstable angina and acute coronary syndrome. This patient's symptoms are unlikely to be associated with hyper- or hypoglycemia. The patient will require admission to the hospital for further monitoring and diagnostic workup. Nonexertional tests, such as dipyridamole-thallium-201 scintigraphy (Choice B), are used to evaluate cardiac perfusion in patients who are unable to exercise. Exercise stress test within 24 hours (Choice C) may be indicated, but first, the patient must be urgently admitted to the hospital for further diagnostic workup and management of unstable angina and acute coronary syndrome. Once further diagnostic tests are completed, the patient's risk can be further delineated using the TIMI score to determine the next most appropriate step in management, which may include stress testing and/or coronary angiography. Antianginal drug therapy now and an exercise stress test in 5 days (Choice D) would unnecessarily delay diagnostic workup of this patient's acute coronary syndrome, which may require coronary angiography and revascularization.

questionStem: A 48-year-old man with alcoholism is brought to the emergency department confused and drowsy 1 hour after he was found on the ground in a park. Examination shows a lateral gaze defect. He has a wide-based ataxic gait. His blood alcohol concentration is less than 0.10 mg/dl. Administration of which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
correctExplanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is characterized by the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. It occurs due to the neurologic consequences from deficiency of vitamin B 1 (thiamine). Patients with alcohol use disorder may mount symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy because of malnutrition secondary to preferential and chronic alcohol consumption. Wernicke encephalopathy is theoretically reversible with administration of high-dose thiamine; if untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome which is characterized by dementia, confabulation, hallucinations, and psychosis. The symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy can mimic alcohol intoxication; however, patients will have a low or undetectable serum ethanol level.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Patients with alcohol use disorder often have deficiencies in folic acid (Choice A), though folic acid deficiency presents with megaloblastic anemia in the setting of impaired DNA synthesis and would not be expected to present with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. The symptoms of hypoglycemia (Choice B) often include confusion and neurologic deficits such as ataxia; however, this patient's presentation is more likely related to a deficiency in vitamin B1. It is important to replenish thiamine with glucose in any patient with alcohol use disorder and hypoglycemia, as relative deficiency of thiamine can theoretically precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. Vitamin B6 (Choice D) deficiency is also common in alcohol use disorder; however, it more commonly presents with neuropathy, dermatitis, glossitis, and seizures. Vitamin B 12 {Choice E) deficiency presents with megaloblastic anemia and neurologic deficits including presentations such as subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and possible dementia, often in a patient with risk factors for vitamin B 12 deficiency such as patients presenting with veganism, malnutrition, Crohn disease, or pernicious anemia. ,.

questionStem: A 57-year-old man with a 5-year history of hypertension comes to the physician for a routine examination . He has a 10-year history of throbbing frontal headaches that occur once to twice monthly and are associated with nausea and sometimes with vomiting . Occasionally, he sees halos around objects during an episode. He attributes the headaches to stress at work . His only medication is enalapril. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. He is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m 2• His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min and regular, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities . Serum studies show : Na+ K+ Cl· HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Glucose Creatinine Ketones Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's increased serum glucose concentration?
correctExplanation: 140 mEq/L 4 mEq/L 100 mEq/L 24 mEq/L 18 mg/dl 265 mg/dl 1.2 mg/dl negative Type 2 diabetes mellitus is common and is caused by increased resistance to insulin signaling. It most frequently occurs in older, obese, and sedentary persons. Type 2 diabetes can be asymptomatic until complications arise as a result of increased blood sugar, which makes screening important. It can be diagnosed through increased Hemoglobin A 10 oral glucose tolerance testing, a random glucose greater than 200 mg/dl with symptoms, or via increased fasting blood glucose greater than 126 mg/dl. Control of blood sugar is important to prevent microvascular complications such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cushing syndrome (Choice A) occurs because of increased cortisol levels and presents with truncal weight gain, fatty deposits around the face and neck, striae, acne, and muscle weakness; vital signs are notable for hypertension, and laboratory workup often reveals hyperglycemia, leukocytosis, and derangements in sodium, bicarbonate, and potassium. Glucagonoma (Choice B) is a rare functional malignancy that secretes glucagon, which raises blood glucose through its normal mechanism of action. Occasionally, glucagonoma can present as a component of multiple endocrine neoplasia. Symptoms are nonspecific and include mild diabetes mellitus and occasionally paraneoplastic rash (e.g., necrolytic migratory erythema) and weight loss. It is not the most likely cause of increased glucose in an older, overweight person with a history of hypertension. Pheochromocytoma (Choice C) is a rare adrenal malignancy that produces catecholamines. Symptoms include paroxysms of anxiety, agitation, diaphoresis, palpitations, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypertension. Somatostatinoma (Choice D) is an uncommon pancreatic malignancy that presents with weight loss, mild diabetes mellitus caused by the suppression of insulin by somatostatin, steatorrhea caused by limited cholecystokinin release, and achlorhydria from inhibition of gastrin. As with many pancreatic malignancies, it is often diagnosed late in its course.

questionStem: A 27-year-old man is found to have a total serum cholesterol concentration of 190 mg/dl at a routine examination . He has no family history of hypertension or premature coronary artery disease. His grandmother was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus at the age of 65 years . Examination shows no abnormalities . In addition to general dietary advice and education concerning risk factors , which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Repeat measurement of serum cholesterol concentration in 5 years
choices.B: Recommend the American Heart Association Step 2 cholesterol-lowering diet

correctExplanation: Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD) has multiple risk factors, including uncontrolled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, obesity, excess alcohol consumption, family history, age, and smoking. Reducing ASCVD is a key step in reducing the likelihood of delayed complications such as heart attacks and strokes. The 2019 guideline from the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease) states that persons with known ASCVD, such as those having experienced a heart attack or stroke, should be started on a high-intensity statin. The guideline makes several recommendations of moderate or high-intensity statin therapy for persons ages 40 to 75 years at risk for ASCVD based on personal medical history, family history, and laboratory evaluation. Routine screening for persons under age 40 years is generally not recommended apart from reasonable surveillance every 4 to 6 years. Those persons ages 20 to 39 years who are not at an increased risk (below 7.5% risk in the next 10 years), a lifetime or 30-year risk target is reasonable in deciding whether or not to initiate lipid-lowering therapy. Lifestyle modification should always be recommended including weight loss, cardiovascular exercise, smoking cessation, safe alcohol consumption, sleep hygiene, and dietary modification for all persons with an increased level of cholesterol or those at risk for ASCVD. While this patient has increased cholesterol, he has no other obvious personal or family risk factors. Lifestyle modifications should be recommended with routine screening and initiation of lipid lowering therapy if his risk subsequently rises.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Recommending the American Heart Association Step 2 cholesterol-lowering diet (Choice B) is aligned to 2019 recommendations from the American Heart Association. General dietary advice and education has already been provided to the patient. Glucose tolerance testing (Choice C) is appropriate for patients in whom a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus is in question. In 2015, the United States Preventive Services Task Force presented a Grade B recommendation for screening for diabetes mellitus in adult patients ages 40 to 70 years. This patient may eventually require screening or diagnosis but does not meet criteria at this time. X-ray of the chest (Choice D) is used to diagnose various cardiothoracic conditions; it is no longer recommended for routine screening. ECG (Choice E) is used to diagnose conditions including but not limited to cardiac arrhythmias, conduction deficits, and myocardial ischemia. ECGs are occasionally used as preoperative screening but are not currently recommended for routine screening in asymptomatic individuals not under investigation for cardiovascular disease.

questionStem: A 65-year-old woman has fatigue, pallor, and glossitis. Hemoglobin concentration is 8 g/dL, and mean corpuscular volume is 115 µm3• Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal. A blood smear is shown . Which of the following is the most likely primary pathophysiologic mechanism causing her anemia?

choices.E: Unbalanced synthesis of a- and 13-globulin chains

correctExplanation: Impaired DNA synthesis occurs in the setting of megaloblastic anemia, characterized by the presence of hypersegmented neutrophils, anemia, and increased mean cell volume (macrocytosis). Commonly, the impairment is due to the absence of required cofactors such as folic acid and cobalamin (vitamin Bd. Malnutrition and alcohol use disorder are common causes of folic acid deficiency, while conditions such as pernicious anemia, Crohn disease, and vegan ism can result in cobalamin deficiency. Symptoms include fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance, with pallor and glossitis found on physical examination. Laboratory evaluation reveals anemia, increased mean cell volume, and normal white cell and platelet indices. The presence of hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear is a characteristic finding in megaloblastic anemia. Treatment includes replacing the deficient vitamin and resolving nutritional deficiencies.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Defective porphyrin metabolism (Choice A) is seen in porphyria. Porphyria can arise from genetic mutations, heavy metal poisoning, and as an adverse effect of some medications. It presents with anemia, and often blistering of the skin when exposed to sunlight. Faulty protein transcription (Choice B) can cause many types of anemia; examples include sickle cell anemia and pyruvate kinase deficiency, both of which typically result in hemolytic, normocytic anemias. Inadequate erythropoietin (Choice D) occurs in chronic end-stage kidney disease because of insufficient production from the peritubular capillary interstitial cells. Without erythropoietin, progenitor cells in the bone marrow are not appropriately stimulated to produce red blood cells, resulting in the development of normocytic, non-hemolytic anemia. Unbalanced synthesis of a- and b-globulin chains (Choice E) defines thalassemia, which classically presents as a microcytic anemia in persons of Mediterranean, Asian, and African descent.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 3-month history of shortness of breath when she climbs stairs. Her shortness of breath resolves after 5 minutes of rest. Her last episode was 3 days ago. She has not had chest pain, palpitations , orthopnea , cough , wheezing , swelling , or difficulty sleeping . She has hypertension and gastroesophageal reflux disease . Current medications include hydrochlorothiazide , omeprazole , and a multivitamin. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 63 kg (140 lb); BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 72/min , respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 144/92 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. There are jugular venous pulsations 3 cm above the sternal angle . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . An ECG shows a left bundle branch block and no primary T-wave changes, which is unchanged from an ECG 1 year ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to determine the cause of this patient's dyspnea?

choices.A: Measurement of serum troponin I concentration

correctExplanation: Stable angina is defined as chest pain (or an anginal equivalent) that occurs with exertion or stress and resolves with rest or nitroglycerin. It indicates that an obstruction to flow exists within a coronary artery (coronary artery disease), which results in myocardial ischemia during a period of increased myocardial oxygen demand. Classically, this occurs from atherosclerotic plaque causing narrowing of a coronary artery, with resultant insufficient supply of blood during periods of increased demand. If such a plaque ulcerates and a thrombus forms, complete occlusion of a coronary artery can result, which can lead to myocardial infarction. Diagnosing inducible cardiac ischemia is first attempted by way of a stress test, either through exercise or pharmacologic stress. An exercise stress echocardiography scan is appropriate for patients who are able to exercise but who have a baseline-abnormal ECG that would make a stress ECG difficult to analyze for ischemia (e.g., such as a baseline bundle-branch block that results in ST-segment repolarization change, or inverted T waves). A stress echocardiogram evaluates for regional wall motion abnormalities suggestive of regional ischemia following induction of stress on the heart via exercise.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum troponin I concentration {Choice A) is appropriate in the diagnosis of an acute coronary syndrome, blunt cardiac injury, myocarditis, or pulmonary embolism. It does not have a role in the diagnosis of stable angina if infarction, injury, or strain on the heart is not suspected. ECG exercise stress test {Choice B) is a first-line screening test in the diagnosis of cardiac ischemia from coronary artery disease, but in patients with an ST-segment baseline ECG abnormality {left or right bundle­ branch block, left ventricular hypertrophy, early repolarization, or ventricular aneurysm), it lacks appropriate sensitivity and specificity. Ventilation-perfusion lung scans {Choice D) are used to assess for mismatches in pulmonary ventilation and perfusion and are most commonly used as a second-line study for pulmonary embolus when a contrast­ enhanced CT angiogram cannot be performed. Coronary angiography {Choice E) is an invasive means of identifying coronary artery disease and is performed through arterial catheterization; it may be required in the diagnosis or treatment of coronary artery disease but would occur following initial noninvasive evaluation in patients not experiencing an acute coronary syndrome.

questionStem: Immediately after undergoing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and dilatation for achalasia, a 32-year-old woman has moderate substernal and midback pain . She has no history of serious illness . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The abdomen is soft and nondistended . Esophagography shows a small leak of contrast from the distal esophagus into the left chest. In addition to intravenous antibiotic therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Placement of an intraluminal esophageal stent
choices.B: Placement of a left chest tube
choices.E: Operative repair of the esoRhageal injury

correctExplanation: The benefits and risks of any procedure must be considered prior to undertaking the procedure. Upper endoscopy is a generally safe procedure, though complications can include bleeding, aspiration, and perforation, and depending on the purpose of the endoscopy, specific complications such as pancreatitis following endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) can occur. In the case of achalasia, the endoscopy was performed to dilate the narrowed lower esophageal sphincter to promote passage of food. Stretching of smooth muscle, stricture, and connective tissue, especially if chronic inflammation from food bolus impaction led to compromise of the stromal strength of the esophageal wall, can lead to perforation. A perforated esophagus is diagnosed on water-soluble contrast esophagography. An esophageal perforation permits translocation of gastrointestinal contents such as food, stomach acid, and bacteria into the mediastinum, which if untreated, can lead to a fatal mediastinitis infection. Management of esophageal perforation is through antibiotics plus emergent surgical repair.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Placement of an intraluminal esophageal stent (Choice A) is used to manage an esophageal obstruction, for example, from an esophageal web, stricture, or malignancy. It does not have a primary role in the management of an acute esophageal perforation. Placement of a left chest tube (Choice B) may be necessary if translocated gastric contents develop into an empyema; however, such complication would not be evident for several days and may be avoided altogether with the use of antibiotics. Nissen fundoplication (Choice C) is a primary surgical treatment for gastroesophageal reflux disease due to incompetence of the lower esophageal sphincter and involves plication of the gastric fund us around the lower esophagus. It does not have an immediate role in repairing an esophageal perforation. Esophagogastrectomy (Choice D) constitutes the removal of a portion of the esophagus and stomach and is often performed in cases of malignancy; it would not have an immediate role in the management of an esophageal perforation.

questionStem: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a lesion on the thigh for 6 months. The lesion is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Malignant melanoma is likely to be present when a skin lesion demonstrates asymmetry, irregular-appearing borders, variable coloration, a diameter greater than 6 mm, and rapid evolution in characteristics. Malignant melanoma has the ability to rapidly invade and metastasize, which carries a poor prognosis when diagnosed late. Any lesion with features suggestive of malignant melanoma should be surgically excised with negative margins and pathologically examined for the depth of dermal invasion.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Observation (Choice A) is inappropriate, as it may result in delay in diagnosis of a potentially lethal malignancy. Radiation therapy (Choice B) may be necessary in treating malignant melanoma, but a diagnosis must first be established. Laser ablation (Choice C) is more frequently used to treat benign cosmetic lesions and would not have a role in the immediate management of malignant melanoma. Electrodessication and curettage (Choice D) may not effectively examine the margins of the lesion, which are important in determining extent of invasion and prognosis.

questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of pain of the fingertips for 1 month . Examination shows plethora and splenomegaly . Laboratory studies show: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows : Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Platelet count Po2 0 2 saturation Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: 20.2 g/dL 14,500/mm 3 with a normal differential 400,000/mm J 92 mm Hg 94% Polycythemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative disorder resulting in increased production of all cell lineages (erythrocyte, leukocyte, and thrombocyte) secondary to a JAK2 mutation. It presents with pruritus, especially after hot showers, secondary to increased mast cell production and degranulation. Additionally, it can present with episodic severe, burning pain with red-blue discoloration secondary to blood clot formation in extremity vessels, referred to as erythromelalgia. The marked increase in red blood cell production and hematocrit can lead to the development of hyperviscosity syndrome, which presents with blurred vision and central nervous system symptoms related to vascular congestion. Examination can show splenomegaly and congestion of vessels seen as plethora. Therapeutic phlebotomy results in decreased red blood cell mass and blood volume, which is the best initial treatment for the patient's symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of chlorambucil (Choice A) is used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia, Hodgkin disease, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. This patient's presentation is most consistent with polycythemia vera. Administration of heparin (Choice B) is appropriate in cases of arterial or venous thrombosis; while this patient may eventually develop a thrombus that requires anticoagulation, at this time there is no evident role for this medication. Thrombopheresis (Choice C) is the selective removal of platelets from blood and is performed during platelet-specific donation or to treat conditions of excess platelets such as essential thrombocythemia when other cell lines are not similarly increased. Splenectomy (Choice E) may have a role in treating patients with polycythemia vera if they have painful splenomegaly or splenic infarction, but barring such complications, it is not a routine next step in the management of polycythemia vera.

questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of increasing nocturnal incontinence that began 2 months ago and now occurs nightly. He has a 20-year history of hypertension treated with verapamil. He has been taking amitriptyline for major depressive disorder since his wife died 3 months ago. His blood pressure is 158/78 mm Hg. There is lower abdominal distention with diffuse tenderness to palpation . Rectal examination shows a moderately enlarged , smooth prostate with no stool in the vault. Neurologic examinations show no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Serum creatinine Urine Protein WBC RBC 1.6 mg/dl 1+ 1-2/hpf 2-4/hpf Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) affects middle-aged and elderly male patients, occurring because of excess growth of tissue in the central prostate causing a lower urinary tract obstruction. BPH presents with urinary dribbling and incontinence, difficulty starting or maintaining a urinary stream, nocturia, the need to frequently urinate, and incomplete voiding. These symptoms are typically insidious in onset, chronic, and progressive. Diagnosis is made on history, physical, and urodynamic testing, along with ruling out alternate diagnoses (eg, prostatic malignancy). Treatment is with supportive care, alpha blockers, 5-a-reductase inhibitors, and/or surgery.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cauda equina syndrome (Choice B) is caused by compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs because of malignancy, trauma (eg, compression fractures with fragment retropulsion), disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal epidural or subdural hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by inability to void. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice C) may present with urinary symptoms in a behavioral context such as volitional voiding at inappropriate times or in inappropriate locations. This patient is not showing any signs of dementia. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (Choice D) presents with symptoms of dementia, urinary incontinence, and ataxia. Urinary tract infection (Choice E) presents with urinary incontinence, dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. It is more common in women than men. Urinalysis typically demonstrates greater than 10 leukocytes per high-power field.

questionStem: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of pain and swelling of her knees. She says she also has had stiffness of her knees, which is worse in the morning. During the past month, she has had progressive , generalized fatigue. On examination , the knees are warm, swollen, and tender. Any attempt at passive movement of the knees produces pain. Her hemoglobin concentration is 10 g/dl , leukocyte count is 10,000/mm 3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 50 mm/h. X-rays of the knees show osteopenia and subcartilaginous cysts around the joints . The joint spaces are intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Pain and swelling of joints, morning stiffness, fatigue, mild anemia, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and x-rays showing periarticular osteopenia and erosions is concerning for an inflammatory arthropathy such as rheumatoid arthritis, pseudogout, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or similar rheumatologic or immunologic disorder. Once secondary causes such as disseminated gonococcal arthritis, Lyme disease, and septic arthritis have been excluded, the first-line treatment is generally with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as ibuprofen.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Oral alendronate (Choice A), a bisphosphonate osteoclast inhibitor, is used in the treatment of osteoporosis and hypercalcemia. It does not have a primary role in the management of an inflammatory arthropathy. Oral colchicine (Choice B) is used in the management of gout, pseudogout, and pericarditis. Gout and pseudogout result from deposition of crystals into the joint space, which trigger an intense inflammatory reaction. Symptoms are more often acute, monoarticular, and severe. Diagnosis is via arthrocentesis. Intra-articular injection of methylprednisolone (Choice D) may have a role in the treatment of inflammatory arthritis but would generally occur after a trial of NSAIDs; additionally, this local treatment would require multiple injections, increasing the risk of infection and discomfort to the patient. Intravenous cefazolin (Choice E) would be appropriate in some cases of septic arthritis if a susceptible pathogen were diagnosed; this patient does not clearly have septic arthritis and antibiotics are inappropriate at this time.

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 1, comes to the physician because of spontaneous discharge from her nipples during the past 3 months . She discontinued breast-feeding her child 1 year ago. She takes no medications . Menses occur at regular 28-day intervals . On physical examination , a milky white discharge can be expressed from both nipples. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Her fasting serum prolactin concentration is 40 ng/ml , and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is within the reference range. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?

choices.A: Application of ice packs to the breasts

correctExplanation: An inappropriate elevation in serum prolactin is defined as hyperprolactinemia and causes production of breast milk and growth of glandular breast tissue. After cessation of breast-feeding, serum prolactin levels typically return to pre-pregnancy levels. Inappropriate elevation of prolactin often arises from a hyperfunctioning anterior pituitary microadenoma and presents with unexpected production of breast milk. Prolactin is negatively regulated by dopamine. Various dopaminergic blocking medications can have galactorrhea as an adverse effect. Further, prolactin is positively regulated by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) and in states of hypothyroidism with upregulated TRH, galactorrhea can also occur. With exclusion of the thyroid and any contributions from dopamine antagonists, further diagnostic evaluation should include an MRI of the brain to assess for the presence of a pituitary adenoma. Treatment is with dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine or cabergoline, and if such medications fail or if a macroadenoma is found, surgical resection of the adenoma is required.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Application of ice packs to the breasts (Choice A) and wearing tight bras (Choice B) are recommendations offered to lactating women approaching the end of breast-feeding or for postpartum women who do not wish to pursue breast-feeding. These measures provide relief of discomfort from engorged breast tissue but have no role in treating hormonal dysregulation from pathologic hyperprolactinemia. Tamoxifen therapy (Choice D), a selective estrogen receptor modulator, is used in the treatment of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer by blocking the trophic action of estrogen on the tumor. It has no role in treating hyperprolactinemia or a pituitary prolactinoma. Vitamin E therapy (Choice E) has been shown to lower prolactin levels in patients with uremia on hemodialysis and has been shown to have an inhibitory effect on pituitary gland hypertrophy; in spite of these findings, it has not been shown to be as effective when compared to dopamine agonists and surgical resection.

questionStem: Four days after undergoing a left total hip replacement , a 75-year-old woman has the rapid onset of chest pain, severe dyspnea, and confusion . Her pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg. A pleural rub is heard at the right lung base. The surgical incision appears to be healing well. There is moderate edema of the left leg. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: Which of the following postoperative treatments is most likely to have prevented this condition?
correctExplanation: pH 7.46 Pco2 28 mm Hg Po2 62 mm Hg Post-operative complications can include infection, bleeding, wound dehiscence, and thromboembolic disease. Care to prevent these complications should be taken during the perioperative period. Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) classically presents with pain and swelling, typically involving one leg, often with a palpable superficial venous cord, and with pain when the extremity is passively flexed at the ankle (the 'Homan' sign). DVT can occur because of venous stasis in an immobilized, post-operative patient, which is often exacerbated by the hypercoagulable inflammatory state following a surgical procedure. If untreated or unrecognized, a DVT can embolize to the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism (PE), which can present as sudden chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and tachypnea. If the PE is large enough to obstruct the outflow from the right side of the heart, hypotension can occur, which is defined as a 'massive' PE. Patients are typically tachypneic, hypoxemic, and demonstrate an acute respiratory alkalosis on arterial blood gas analysis. Postoperative anticoagulation using pharmacologic (eg anticoagulant therapy) or mechanical prophylaxis (eg frequent ambulation, sequential lower extremity compression) can reduce the incidence of DVT and PE.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aspirin (Choice A) is an antiplatelet agent commonly used as prophylaxis against arterial thrombotic phenomena involving the coronary arteries (eg, myocardial infarction) and cerebral arteries (eg, cerebrovascular accidents). It does not have a recognized role in the prevention of DVT/PE. Administration of cefoxitin (Choice B), a second-generation cephalosporin, can be used for the treatment of common gram-positive, and some gram-negative pathogens, such as in pelvic inflammatory disease. It does not have a role in the prevention of DVT/PE. Administration of oxygen (Choice C) has a role in treating hypoxemia secondary to PE but has no role in the prevention of DVT/PE. Use of incentive spirometry (Choice E) has been shown to prevent post-operative atelectasis along with post-operative pneumonia. It does not have a role in the prevention of DVT/PE.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. She was the restrained front seat passenger . Her neck was immobilized in a cervical collar at the scene . On arrival , she reports neck pain and pain in her right forearm . Her pulse is 80/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. Examination of the right upper extremity shows swelling and crepitus . She is able to actively extend the proximal and distal interphalangeal joints but not the metacarpophalangeal joints of her right hand or wrist. The remainder of the examination shows no other abnormalities . Plain x-rays show a midshaft fracture of the humerus . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The radial nerve courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove. It is often injured in displaced midshaft humerus fractures, with resulting wrist drop. The radial nerve supplies motor fibers to the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles within the posterior compartment of the forearm and sensory fibers to the dorsum of the forearm, wrist, and hand. It does not innervate the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Injury to the nerve at the mid-diaphyseal humerus causes extensor muscle loss at the hand and wrist, weakness of forearm supination, the presence of wrist drop, and sensory loss over the posterior forearm, dorsum of the hand, and posterior thumb, index, middle, and radial-half of the ring finger.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Brachia! plexus injury (Choice A), depending on the location within the plexus, would involve motor and sensory loss of multiple nerves. A mononeuropathy would be unlikely. Compartment syndrome (Choice B) presents with pain, paresthesia, paresis, poikilothermia, pallor, and pulselessness. It occurs because of increased pressure from swelling or hemorrhage within a fixed-space myofascial compartment. When the pressure approaches or exceeds diastolic blood pressure, blood flow becomes impaired. The compartment and any downstream-supplied structures can become ischemic. With an otherwise normal exam, the localization of the patient's findings to radial nerve injury is much more likely. Herniated cervical disc (Choice C) can occur from traumatic injury and is a known cause of cervical radiculopathy. Usually, one single nerve root is affected, and it commonly presents with pain in a radicular pattern. Weakness of muscles innervated by multiple cervical spinal levels would be less likely outside of catastrophic injury to the cervical spine. Median nerve injury (Choice D) presents with weakness involving the flexor compartment of the forearm, thenar eminence, and first two lumbrical muscles, along with diminished sensation over the anterior forearm and lateral hand.

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because of confusion and sleepiness for the past 12 hours. She has mild hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide but is otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 150/100 mm Hg. On examination , she is obtunded and confused. There is no jugular venous distention when she is supine. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . There are no focal neurologic signs. Serum studies show: Intravenous infusion of which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
correctExplanation: Na• K+ Ca2• Urea nitrogen Glucose Creatinine Albumin 146 mEq/L 5.0 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 40 mg/dl 105 mg/dl 1.8 mg/dl 3.1 g/dl Acute hypercalcemia can present with a broad spectrum of symptoms and can be life-threatening because of its effect on neuronal conduction, the cardiac action potential, kidney function, and volume status. It can result from an exacerbation of known hypercalcemia (e.g., in cases of bony metastatic disease with increased osteoclast activity) or as a new diagnosis caused by an acute electrolyte derangement (e.g., excessive intake of calcium in the form of antacid medication). Hypercalcemia can induce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus resulting in excessive renal water losses. Treatment includes fluid resuscitation to prevent renal failure, promoting renal excretion of calcium, reducing intestinal absorption of calcium, inhibiting bony destruction, and, if necessary, renal replacement therapy with dialysis. Treatment therefore begins with infusion of 0.9% saline to restore intravascular volume and dilute serum calcium, followed by administration of osteoclast inhibitors such as bisphosphonates and possibly calcitonin if further medications are required to reduce calcium levels.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Albumin (Choice A) is used as a resuscitation colloid in cases of known hypoalbuminemia, such as liver failure or nephrotic syndrome. It supplies minimal intravascular volume directly, but rather, draws fluid into the intravascular space through oncotic pressure. Such equilibration takes time, making it a suboptimal colloid in managing symptomatic hypercalcemia. Furosemide (Choice B), a loop diuretic, acts at the kidney to promote fluid and electrolyte losses, including calcium. It has a role in the management of hypercalcemia but would be used following adequate volume resuscitation, not before. Glucose and insulin (Choice C) are a combined therapy used to shift potassium into cells in cases of acute hyperkalemia while maintaining normoglycemia. This patient's potassium level is within normal limits; immediate intervention is not required at this time. Oral sodium phosphate (Choice E) has an adjunct role in binding calcium in the GI tract, preventing further absorption, but does not have a role in the abrupt lowering of serum calcium levels. Intravenous phosphate has also been shown to bind calcium in the serum; however, the resulting insoluble calcium-phosphate product can deposit throughout tissues. This treatment may lead to additional organ dysfunction and should be avoided if possible.

questionStem: A 40-year-old man with alcoholism has had a low-grade fever, malaise , and cough productive of purulent sputum for 2 weeks and hemoptysis for 24 hours; during this period, he has had a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. His temperature is 37 .8°C (100°F) . Hematocrit is 33%, and leukocyte count is 15,000/mm 3• An x-ray of the chest shows a large cavitary lesion with an air-fluid level in the superior segment of the right lower lobe of the lung. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Aspiration pneumonia is characterized by fever, cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, malaise, and chest discomfort following an aspiration event; untreated or complicated aspiration pneumonia can lead to the development of a lung abscess, especially with the pathogen Klebsiel/a pneumoniae. Patients at higher risk for aspiration include those with impaired airway-protective reflexes (eg, stroke, myasthenia gravis, depressed mental status), those with frequent or forceful emesis (eg, alcohol use disorder, cyclic vomiting syndrome), or those with abnormal pharyngeal or airway anatomy (eg, malignancy, tracheo-esophageal fistula). These patients are more likely to aspirate gastric contents into the lung, which results in bacterial seeding with gastrointestinal or oral flora and can lead to pneumonia. Frequently, aspiration occurs in a dependent segment of the lung such as bilateral lower lobes when erect or the lingula, right middle lobe, and superior segments of the lower lobes while lying down. Pulmonary abscesses often present with low-grade fevers, weight loss, anemia, and leukocytosis. On chest x-ray, air-fluid levels are seen within the abscess cavity. Treatment is with antibiotics, prevention of recurrent aspiration, and source control with surgical resection or percutaneous drainage.

Homeless persons, patients suffering from alcohol use disorder, incarcerated patients, those from endemic areas (eg, Africa, South America), and those living in close contact are more likely to contract tuberculosis (Choice E).
